record.paper_title: Some open problems in mathematical relativity
record.original_question: Can one find an exact solution of the Einstein equations representing two orbiting bodies, and is the two-body system unstable in Einstein gravity?

evidence.quote: Fi.nd an exact solution of the Einstein equations which represents two orbiting bodies. Is the 2-body system unstable in Einstein gravity?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In general relativity, spacetime is modeled as a 4-dimensional Lorentzian manifold $(M,g)$ whose metric $g$ satisfies the Einstein field equations
$$ R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac{1}{2} R\, g_{\mu\nu} = 8\pi T_{\mu\nu}, $$
where $R_{\mu\nu}$ is the Ricci tensor of $g$, $R$ its scalar curvature, and $T_{\mu\nu}$ the stress-energy tensor of the matter content.

(a) Exhibit, in closed analytic form, an exact solution $(M,g)$ of the Einstein field equations (coupled to a reasonable matter model, e.g.\ two localized bodies modeled as perfect fluids or as point-like sources, or as a vacuum solution outside two compact bodies) that describes two gravitating bodies in mutual bound orbital motion about one another. The solution should genuinely represent a two-body bound configuration (as opposed to a test particle on a fixed background such as Schwarzschild or Kerr).

(b) Decide whether the two-body system in Einstein gravity is dynamically unstable: namely, prove or disprove that any such bound two-body configuration must inspiral and merge (e.g.\ due to gravitational-wave emission or other relativistic effects) so that no truly stationary or periodic two-body bound state exists in pure Einstein gravity.
artifact.status_search_result: The relativistic two-body problem is widely regarded as having no known exact closed-form solution; only approximate (post-Newtonian, effective-one-body) and numerical solutions are available. Wikipedia and standard references confirm that, due to the nonlinearity of the Einstein equations, an exact analytic two-body solution is not known, and the dynamical instability (inspiral via gravitational radiation) is expected but not established by an exact solution. The problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: Two-body problem in general relativity - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The field equations governing this curvature are nonlinear and therefore difficult to solve in a closed form. No exact solutions of the Kepler problem have been found; instead approximation methods such as the post-Newtonian expansion and numerical relativity are used.
status_evidence.claim: No exact closed-form two-body solution of the Einstein equations is known; only approximations and numerical solutions exist.
